notes.claim: Connecting a control circuit to an SCR's gate lets the sine wave be chopped at any point, giving time-proportioned power control to a load.
For a smaller DC voltage the trigger pulse is delayed more, though the delay also lowers the converter's input power factor.
A soft starter fires its thyristors to ramp the voltage from 0 to rated, which limits the motor's starting current.
For i5: firing a thyristor with a pulse on its gate latches it on; this triggering or firing is the usual way to turn one on.
For i5: a thyristor turns off when its current falls below the holding current, not when the gate signal goes.
For i5: on AC a thyristor turns off just before the current's zero crossing (natural commutation) and must be fired again in the next cycle.
For i5: replacing a rectifier's diodes with thyristors makes a controlled rectifier, its DC power set by when they are fired.
For i5: with a fully controlled single-phase bridge the average DC is positive below a 90 degree firing angle and negative above it, when power flows from the DC side back to the AC supply.
For i5: a triac behaves like two thyristors connected in inverse parallel, so it controls both halves of the AC.
For i5: triac lamp dimmers are meant for resistive loads only and should not be used as a motor speed controller.
For i5: thyristor-controlled rectifiers are used to charge nickel-cadmium or lead-acid batteries while supplying DC loads.
For i5: lead-acid batteries are charged by the constant current, constant voltage (CCCV) method.
For i5: a motor started direct on line draws usually 6 to 8 times its rated current, sometimes more than 10 times.
For i5: lead-acid batteries on charge give off hydrogen, explosive in air between 4.1 and 72 percent hydrogen.
For i5: a gate turn-off thyristor (GTO) is a variant of the SCR designed to be turned off through its gate.
